title: WE WRESTLE NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD — SO WHY ARE YOU DESTROYING THE PEOPLE YOU WERE CALLED TO LOVE?
paragraphs: WE WRESTLE NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD — SO WHY ARE YOU DESTROYING THE PEOPLE YOU WERE CALLED TO LOVE?

The enemy has convinced too many Christians to fight their spouses, abandon their families, attack their brothers and sisters, and hate the very people Jesus died to save. But what if the person you have been fighting is not your real enemy—and the battle you keep losing is happening somewhere you have forgotten to look?
There is something heartbreaking happening in Christian homes, churches, friendships, and families.
And the frightening part?
Some of us are calling it spiritual warfare.
A husband walks out of the bedroom after another argument, convinced his wife is the reason he has no peace.
A wife lies awake beside a man she once prayed to marry, silently wondering how someone she loves so deeply can make her feel so alone.
A mother cries because her child no longer wants anything to do with God.
Two believers stop speaking because one misunderstood a message, one refused to apologize, and both are waiting for the other to humble themselves first.
A church splits.
A friendship dies.
A family stops gathering around the same table.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pain, people who carry Bibles in their hands begin carrying bitterness in their hearts.
They still pray.
They still worship.
They still share Scriptures.
But mention a certain person's name, and something inside them changes.
Their voice hardens.
Their compassion disappears.
Their wounds begin speaking louder than their faith.
And perhaps the most dangerous part is that they can explain exactly why their anger is justified.
Because they were hurt.
Because they were betrayed.
Because they were disrespected.
Because somebody lied.
Because somebody who should have protected them became the reason they needed healing.
And maybe that somebody is the very person who came to your mind when you read the title.
Don't rush past that.
Because what comes next may challenge the way you have been looking at your pain.
You can be genuinely wounded by another human being and still be deceived about who your ultimate enemy is.
The hurt may be real.
The betrayal may be real.
The injustice may be real.
But the person responsible for that hurt is still a human being made in the image of God.
And if you forget that, the wound someone gave you can become the place where bitterness begins reshaping you.
The apostle Paul wrote something that many Christians have memorized but far fewer have allowed to govern their relationships.
"For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."
— Ephesians 6:12, King James Version
Read those first few words again.
We wrestle not against flesh and blood.
Not your husband.
Not your wife.
Not your rebellious child.
Not the friend who betrayed your confidence.
Not the church member who embarrassed you.
Not the person who mocked your faith.
Not even the person who openly hates you.
Paul was not saying that human beings never commit evil or that wrongdoing should go unanswered.
He was revealing something deeper about the nature of the Christian struggle.
Behind the visible conflicts of life, believers face an unseen spiritual opposition that cannot be defeated by hatred, revenge, manipulation, or human strength.
And if you fight a spiritual battle with the weapons of your wounded flesh, you may end up destroying relationships while believing you are defending righteousness.
The original Greek makes Paul's words even more striking.
The expression translated "we wrestle" comes from the Greek word πάλη (palē), meaning wrestling or struggle.
Paul uses the language of close combat.
Not a distant disagreement.
Not a casual inconvenience.
A struggle.
Something exhausting.
Something that demands endurance.
Something that can leave you feeling as though you have nothing left.
But notice the distinction Paul makes.
He writes:
οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα
ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka
Literally, the wording conveys: "Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh."
The Greek expression αἷμα καὶ σάρκα (haima kai sarka) refers to human beings in their mortal, bodily existence.
Paul is drawing a line between human opponents and the spiritual powers that oppose God's purposes.
He is not denying human responsibility.
He is identifying the deeper nature of the believer's warfare.
That distinction matters.
Because there is a terrible difference between confronting someone's sin and deciding that the person themselves is beyond redemption.
There is a difference between establishing a necessary boundary and allowing hatred to become your identity.
There is a difference between seeking justice and secretly craving revenge.
And there is a difference between discerning evil and treating every difficult person as though they are possessed by it.
Not every argument is a demonic attack.
Not every disagreement is spiritual oppression.
Sometimes people are selfish.
Sometimes people misunderstand each other.
Sometimes trauma affects the way someone responds.
Sometimes pride keeps two people from saying the words that could begin a difficult conversation.
Sometimes we are simply wrong.
And sometimes the person we have spent weeks praying for God to change is not the only person who needs to repent.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is much easier to pray, "Lord, expose what is wrong with them," than to pray, "Lord, show me what is wrong in me."
It is easier to identify someone else's arrogance than to recognize our own.
It is easier to remember every harsh word they spoke than to admit the cruelty of the words we spoke afterward.
It is easier to ask God to defend us than to surrender our desire to punish them.
And if that sentence made you uncomfortable, perhaps it touched something that deserves prayer rather than another excuse.
Jesus did not call His followers to pretend evil does not exist.
He called them to refuse to become evil in response.
"Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
— Matthew 5:44, KJV
Think about how radical that command is.
Jesus did not say, "Love only the people who understand you."
He did not say, "Pray only for the people who apologize."
He did not say, "Show kindness only when the other person deserves it."
He told His disciples to love their enemies.
Not because their enemies were innocent.
Not because their actions were acceptable.
But because the children of God are called to reflect the character of their Father.
And the Father is merciful.
Even when we have been difficult to love.
Even when we have resisted His correction.
Even when we have given Him every reason to judge us.
There is a moment in the Gospel that exposes just how different the kingdom of Jesus is from the instincts of our wounded hearts.
It happened in a garden.
The night Jesus was betrayed.
Judas arrived with the crowd sent to arrest Him.
There were weapons.
There was tension.
There was treachery.
And Peter, watching the situation unfold, drew a sword.
He struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear.
John tells us the servant's name was Malchus.
And then Jesus did something that should make every angry Christian reconsider what it means to fight for God.
He stopped Peter.
"Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?"
— John 18:11, KJV
Luke also records that Jesus touched the wounded man's ear and healed him (Luke 22:51).
Let that scene settle into your heart.
Peter was ready to injure someone in defense of Jesus.
Jesus was willing to heal the person Peter had injured.
Peter saw an enemy standing in front of him.
Jesus saw a human being whose suffering He could relieve.
And here is what makes the moment even more astonishing.
Jesus was not confused about what was happening.
He knew He was being betrayed.
He knew He was being arrested unjustly.
He knew the suffering ahead of Him.
He was not surrendering because He lacked power.
He was submitting to the Father's redemptive purpose.
The Son of God did not need Peter's violence to secure His victory.
And sometimes, neither does the truth need our cruelty to defend it.
That does not mean Christians must remain silent when confronted with evil.
It means our methods must not contradict the Lord we claim to serve.
If defending your faith requires you to abandon the character of Christ, something has gone terribly wrong in the way you are fighting.
Perhaps you need to hear that because you have been fighting for your marriage with insults.
Fighting for your reputation with gossip.
Fighting for your ministry with resentment.
Fighting for your dignity by humiliating someone else.
Fighting for the truth while refusing to speak it in love.
And somewhere along the way, the fight became more important than the people involved.
You began measuring victory by whether the other person suffered.
Whether they were embarrassed.
Whether they finally admitted you were right.
Whether everybody else discovered what they did to you.
But the kingdom of God does not define victory that way.
Romans 12:21 says:
"Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
Not surrender to evil.
Not excuse evil.
Not conceal evil.
Overcome it.
And overcome it with good.
That may mean speaking the truth when silence would be easier.
It may mean confronting sin without humiliating the sinner.
It may mean refusing to participate in gossip even when you possess information that could ruin someone's reputation.
It may mean protecting a child from a dangerous person.
It may mean leaving an abusive environment, seeking help, and allowing appropriate authorities to intervene.
It may mean telling someone, "I forgive you, but I cannot trust you with the same access to my life right now."
Because forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Forgiveness releases the claim to personal vengeance.
Reconciliation involves the rebuilding of a relationship, which may require repentance, truth, accountability, and demonstrated change.
Trust is not automatically restored because someone says, "I'm sorry."
And biblical peacemaking does not require victims to return to danger.
When Paul says, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Romans 12:18), those opening words matter.
If it be possible.
Peace is worth pursuing.
But peace cannot always be established by one person alone.
You can refuse hatred without pretending someone is safe.
You can pray for an enemy while maintaining distance.
You can desire someone's repentance without granting them permission to continue harming you.
And you can love someone without allowing them to control you.
Jesus Himself sometimes withdrew from those who sought to harm Him.
Love is not the absence of discernment.
It is the refusal to surrender your heart to hatred.
But there is another side to this message.
And for some of us, it is the harder side.
What if the person who has become difficult to love is not an abuser or a dangerous enemy?
What if they are simply someone who disappointed you?
Someone who disagreed with you?
Someone who did not respond the way you expected?
Someone who failed to read your mind?
Someone who made a mistake and has been trying to make it right?
What if the relationship is dying not because reconciliation is impossible, but because pride has made humility feel unbearable?
What if you have been calling it discernment when it is actually resentment?
What if you have been calling it protecting your peace when you are really punishing someone with silence?
What if you have been calling it standing for truth when you are simply refusing to listen?
Those questions are not accusations.
They are invitations to examine our hearts before God.
Because the Bible warns us about the destructive power of unresolved anger.
"Neither give place to the devil."
— Ephesians 4:27, KJV
That verse appears in a passage where Paul addresses anger, truthful speech, work, kindness, forgiveness, and the way believers treat one another.
The Greek word translated "place" is τόπος (topos).
It can mean a place, space, or opportunity.
In this context, Paul warns believers not to give the devil an opening through sinful responses to anger.
He is not teaching that every angry emotion is demonic.
In fact, the preceding verse says:
"Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
— Ephesians 4:26, KJV
Anger itself can be a response to genuine injustice.
But anger can also become a doorway to sinful behavior when it is cherished, weaponized, or allowed to rule the heart.
And that is where a spiritual battle can quietly become a personal tragedy.
The original injury may have been caused by someone else.
But what you choose to cultivate afterward matters.
Bitterness does not always arrive looking like bitterness.
Sometimes it arrives looking like a perfectly reasonable decision never to forgive.
Sometimes it sounds like rehearsing the same offense every night.
Sometimes it feels like satisfaction when the person who hurt you experiences misfortune.
Sometimes it hides behind a smile at church while silently hoping another believer will fail.
And sometimes it becomes so familiar that you stop noticing how much space it occupies in your life.
You can become so consumed with proving that somebody else was wrong that you stop asking God to make you right before Him.
And the enemy does not need to make you abandon your Bible if he can persuade you to ignore the parts that confront your hatred.
That is why the spiritual armor Paul describes in Ephesians 6 matters so deeply.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness of the gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The word of God.
Prayer.
Notice what is missing.
Revenge.
Cruelty.
Character assassination.
Pride.
Contempt.
The weapons Paul describes are not permission to wage war against people.
They are God's provision for standing firm against spiritual evil.
The believer does not overcome darkness by becoming another expression of it.
And nowhere is that truth more clearly displayed than at the cross.
Consider what happened to Jesus.
He was betrayed by a friend.
Denied by a disciple.
Abandoned by many who had followed Him.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Struck.
Condemned.
Crucified.
If anyone could have claimed the right to retaliate, it was the sinless Son of God.
And yet, as Luke records His crucifixion, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, KJV

A textual note matters here: this prayer appears in the traditional Greek text and many ancient manuscripts, while some early manuscripts omit it. It is preserved in the King James Version and many modern Bibles, sometimes with a manuscript note.
The prayer expresses the mercy that shines throughout the Gospel accounts.
Jesus did not deny the wickedness of what was being done.
He did not call injustice righteousness.
He did not suggest that sin was harmless.
He bore the consequences of human sin while fulfilling the Father's saving purpose.
And the cross reveals something that human pride finds difficult to accept.
We are not merely people who have been wounded by the sins of others.
We are also sinners who need mercy ourselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we became deserving.
Not after we repaired every wrong.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy of forgiveness.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And a few verses later, Paul says that we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies (Romans 5:10).
Enemies.
That word should silence some of our self-righteousness.
Because before we ask how God could expect us to love difficult people, we should remember how merciful He has been to us.
We were not saved because we were easier to love than everyone else.
We were saved by grace.
Through faith.
Because Jesus Christ did what we could never do for ourselves.
He lived without sin.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not a message that simply teaches wounded people how to behave better.
Not a religious strategy for maintaining pleasant relationships.
It is the announcement that God has acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners, defeat the powers of evil, forgive the repentant, and make new life possible.
And that new life changes how we see other people.
The person who hurt you is not automatically innocent.
But neither are they beyond God's ability to save.
The person you dislike may still be someone Christ is calling to repentance.
The family member who has wandered from faith may still return.
The friend who failed you may still learn humility.
And the person whose name causes your heart to tighten may be someone you need to entrust to God's justice rather than your own revenge.
You do not know every chapter God may yet write in another person's life.
Consider Saul of Tarsus.
Before he became known as the apostle Paul, he persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He entered homes and dragged away believers.
He threatened followers of Jesus.
If you had been among the Christians living in fear of Saul, you would have had very real reasons to regard him as dangerous.
And he was.
The early believers did not invent that danger.
But on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus confronted Saul.
And the persecutor became a preacher of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
That transformation did not erase the suffering Saul had caused.
Nor did it mean believers were required to trust him immediately.
Acts 9:26 records that the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him and did not believe he was a disciple.
Their caution was understandable.
Barnabas later helped them understand what God had done.
This is what grace looks like when it enters a story marked by scandal.
It does not pretend the past never happened.
It does not call evil good.
It confronts sin and opens the door to transformation.
The same man who once pursued Christians became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
The same hands associated with persecution would eventually write letters encouraging believers to love one another.
And the same Paul who knew the violence of religious zeal would write:
Do you see it?
The man who once fought people in the name of God learned that the true battle could not be won by destroying human beings.
That is the kind of grace that rewrites a life.
And maybe, just maybe, it is the grace your own story desperately needs.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying years of resentment toward a parent who never apologized.
Perhaps you have been praying for a spouse while quietly becoming bitter toward them.
Perhaps someone in your church betrayed your trust, and you have been unable to separate their actions from your understanding of God.
Perhaps you were wounded by a Christian who spoke beautifully about love but treated you cruelly.
Perhaps you have been so disappointed by people who claim to represent Jesus that you are beginning to pull away from Jesus Himself.
If that is you, please hear this.
The failure of someone who bears Christ's name is not the measure of Christ's character.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy that wounded you.
He is not the cruelty that was justified with Scripture.
He is not the manipulation that was disguised as spiritual authority.
He is not the betrayal that made you afraid to trust again.
Look at Him in the Gospels.
Look at how He treated the broken.
How He confronted the proud.
How He welcomed repentant sinners.
How He defended the vulnerable.
How He spoke truth without surrendering to wickedness.
How He went to the cross for people who could never save themselves.
That is the Savior you are being invited to follow.
Not a perfect religious community.
Not a flawless spiritual leader.
Not a life free from human disappointment.
Jesus Christ.
And He is worthy of your trust even when people have proven unworthy of it.
Maybe you have been waiting for the person who hurt you to change before you allow God to begin changing you.
Maybe you have been telling yourself that healing cannot start until you receive an apology.
Maybe you believe that if you stop rehearsing what happened, the injustice will somehow disappear.
But releasing vengeance does not erase the truth.
God sees what happened.
He sees what was done in secret.
He sees the tears nobody else noticed.
He sees the years you spent trying to understand why someone you loved treated you that way.
And He does not ask you to call darkness light.
He calls you to bring the darkness into His presence.
To seek truth.
To pursue justice where justice is needed.
To establish boundaries where boundaries are necessary.
To repent where you have sinned.
And to surrender the final judgment of souls to Him.
That surrender is not weakness.
It is faith.
Faith that God's justice is greater than your revenge.
Faith that His mercy is greater than your bitterness.
Faith that your future does not have to remain chained to what somebody did in your past.
And faith that Jesus can transform even the parts of your heart that have become hard through suffering.
Perhaps the most important battle you face today is not another argument with the person who wounded you.
Perhaps it is the battle to remain faithful to Christ while carrying a wound that still hurts.
To speak truth without hatred.
To protect yourself without becoming cruel.
To seek reconciliation without compromising safety.
To forgive without denying reality.
To love without surrendering discernment.
To resist the devil without demonizing human beings.
And to remember that you, too, stand in desperate need of grace.
James 4:7 says:
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Then resist the devil.
We cannot successfully resist evil while proudly refusing the authority of the Lord.
And one of the hardest forms of submission is allowing God to confront the anger we have grown comfortable defending.
So before you send that message...
Before you post that accusation...
Before you tell another person what somebody did...
Before you decide that reconciliation is impossible...
Before you use the Bible to justify the resentment you have been feeding...
Ask yourself something.
Am I trying to honor Jesus?
Or am I trying to make somebody pay?
Am I pursuing truth?
Or am I pursuing humiliation?
Am I protecting what is right?
Or am I protecting my pride?
Am I resisting evil?
Or am I allowing evil to reshape the way I treat people?
And if you discover something in your heart that needs repentance, do not run from God.
Run toward Him.
Because conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to return.
First John 1:9 reminds believers:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
There is mercy for the wounded person who has become bitter.
There is mercy for the proud person who finally admits they were wrong.
There is mercy for the Christian who has been using spiritual language to disguise personal resentment.
There is mercy for the one who needs to apologize.
There is mercy for the one who needs to establish a boundary.
And there is mercy for the person who has been running from God because the failures of people made faith feel unbearable.
That mercy has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And He does not merely offer to improve your behavior.
He calls you to die to the old life and walk in newness of life through Him.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will never be simply, "Be a better person."
Our message is that sinners need a Savior.
Wounded hearts need the truth of Christ.
Broken relationships need more than religious appearances.
And a world exhausted by hatred needs to encounter the Gospel of reconciliation.
Second Corinthians 5:18 teaches that God reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ and entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to His servants.
That ministry does not mean every broken human relationship will be restored.
But it does mean that people who have received reconciliation with God should not treat hatred as their permanent home.
We are ambassadors of Christ.
Not ambassadors of resentment.
Not ambassadors of revenge.
Not ambassadors of endless arguments.
We belong to the One who makes all things new.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been trying to keep hidden, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply agreeing with it.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your pain.
You do not have to name the person who hurt you.
You do not have to expose a private family struggle.
There is no shame in admitting that following Jesus can be difficult when the heart is hurting.
Sometimes those few honest words become the beginning of a conversation, a prayer, or an encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Maybe they will discover that repentance is not humiliation.
It is a return to the God whose mercy is greater than our sin.
There is also someone in your life who may need to read this message today.
Perhaps it is a family member caught in an exhausting conflict.
A friend who is slowly losing faith because of what another Christian did.
A couple who have forgotten they are meant to face their problems together rather than treat each other as the problem.
A believer who has confused righteous conviction with personal hatred.
Or someone who has been hurt so deeply that they no longer believe grace can reach their situation.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable today.

But because the next time anger rises, the next time betrayal stings, or the next time you are tempted to make another human being the ultimate enemy, you may need to remember what Scripture actually says.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, genuine encouragement, repentance, healing, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Not shallow inspiration that disappears when life becomes difficult.
But spiritual nourishment that calls us back to the Savior.
These resources are meant to help believers study Scripture, deepen their faith, strengthen their families, and continue learning long after they finish reading an article.
And if Gospel Warrior has become part of your spiritual journey, I would also like to invite you to consider something prayerfully.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
Not because a monthly payment makes you more faithful than a believer who cannot afford one.
And certainly not because the grace of Jesus can ever be bought.
The Gospel is a gift.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works or financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Paul speaks about supporting those who proclaim the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 9:14, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from the heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
These products can be reminders of the truths we want to carry into ordinary life, but they are never substitutes for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or obedience to Jesus.
It is an opportunity to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
And our prayer is that every resource, every article, every testimony, and every act of generosity would ultimately direct attention away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
To remind the ashamed that repentance is possible.
To remind the broken that grace is real.
To remind the bitter that freedom does not have to wait for revenge.
To remind the wandering that the Father still calls sinners to return.
And to remind the church that we cannot proclaim the Gospel of reconciliation while celebrating the destruction of the people Christ commands us to love.
Now, before you leave this article, there is one last picture I want you to carry with you.
Imagine standing before Jesus with every wound you have carried.
Every betrayal.
Every unanswered question.
Every cruel word.
Every sleepless night.
Every moment you wondered whether you would ever be whole again.
Imagine bringing Him the names of the people who hurt you.
And imagine also bringing Him the moments when your own heart responded with sin.
Not to deny what happened.
Not to minimize your suffering.
But to place the entire truth before the One who sees perfectly and judges righteously.
You do not need to imagine that Jesus will ask you to pretend evil was good.
He never does.
But Scripture assures us that the final victory belongs to Him.
He will judge evil.
He will make all things new.
And those who belong to Him will not carry the wounds of this fallen world forever.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That is where Christian hope leads.
Not to endless conflict.
Not to permanent bitterness.
Not to a life defined by the worst thing somebody did to you.
But to the risen Christ, who will bring His people into the fullness of His kingdom.
Until that day, we wrestle.
We pray.
We resist evil.
We speak truth.
We seek justice.
We forgive as Christ has forgiven us.
We repent when our own hearts go astray.
We love even when love is costly.
And we remember that the person standing in front of us is not the ultimate enemy Scripture tells us to fight.
The devil would gladly see human relationships destroyed by lies, hatred, temptation, and sin.
But Jesus calls His people to stand firm in truth, righteousness, faith, prayer, and the Gospel of peace.
So put down the weapon of personal vengeance.
Not the truth.
Not wisdom.
Not the boundaries that keep you safe.
Not the courage to confront wrongdoing.
Put down the hatred that has begun to poison your own heart.
And take up the armor God has actually given you.
Because the cross of Jesus Christ has already revealed that the greatest victory is not achieved by becoming more ruthless than our enemies.
It is found in the saving work of the One who conquered sin and death through His sacrifice and resurrection.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, come to Him in repentance and faith.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have been wounded, bring your suffering to Him and seek the help you need.
If you have been consumed by bitterness, ask Him to teach you the freedom of entrusting justice to God.
And if there is a relationship where humble, safe, truthful reconciliation is possible, perhaps today is the day to take the first faithful step.
You may not be able to change the other person.
You may not be able to rewrite what happened.
You may not receive the apology you hoped for.
But through Jesus Christ, your story does not have to end where the injury began.
That is our hope.
That is the Gospel we proclaim.
That is why we keep pointing people back to the cross.
Because no scandal is greater than the power of Christ to redeem a repentant sinner.
No human failure can cancel the truth of His resurrection.
And no darkness can finally overcome the kingdom of the risen King.
The person who wounded you may have written one of the darkest chapters of your life—but do not hand them the pen that writes the rest of your soul.
